title: Scientists can now 'watermark' AI-generated proteins to deter bioweapon creation. But will it really work?

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: A student journalist interviews a university biosecurity officer about AI protein design and safety oversight.

script.en: Professor Lane, thanks for meeting me. I'm writing for the campus science magazine about the new AI protein-design tools. Some students are worried these could be misused.

It's a legitimate concern. The same software that helps us design a novel enzyme for medicine could, in principle, be redirected toward harmful agents. That's why we now need an ethics review before any generative protein work on campus.
So every student project gets screened?

Not every single one. Routine coursework is exempt. But if a project involves creating sequences not found in nature, the researcher must submit a risk assessment. We check whether the design could plausibly enhance virulence or evade existing countermeasures.
I've read that some labs are embedding hidden signatures into AI-generated proteins. Does our university use that?

We're watching the technology closely, but we haven't adopted it yet. The signatures can be stripped out fairly easily, so they're more of a deterrent than a guarantee. For now, human review remains our primary safeguard.
Critics say that kind of review slows down legitimate research. How do you respond?

There's certainly a cost in time. But the review process usually takes days, not months, and it has caught at least two proposals that were poorly justified. I'd argue the delay is modest compared with the potential consequences of an accident or deliberate misuse.
What about international collaboration? A lab overseas might not follow the same rules.

That's the hard part. Biosecurity can't stop at national borders. We're pushing for shared screening standards, but progress is slow because institutions guard their autonomy. Still, I'm cautiously optimistic that the norm is shifting.
One last question: what should a student do if they suspect a project is risky?
Speak to the ethics committee directly. You don't need proof, just a reasonable concern. Early reporting is far better than waiting until something goes wrong.

script.en: In recent years, AI has changed how scientists design proteins. Proteins are the molecular machines that do most jobs in living cells. AI tools predict how amino acid chains fold into 3D shapes. This lets them create proteins that do not exist in nature. These proteins could help medicine and industry, and but the same power raises hard questions about security. In theory, a designed protein could be turned into a harmful agent. To reduce this risk, researchers have proposed hiding markers, or watermarks, in AI-generated proteins. The idea is simple, and if a protein carries a detectable signature, authorities can trace its origin. They can also flag suspicious designs for closer inspection, and early tests suggest these watermarks can be found with high accuracy. The protein's function also stays largely intact, and however, independent experts remain cautious, and they point out that watermarks are fragile. A determined user can change the amino acid sequence or adjust the molecular structure. Then the signature disappears, and once removed, the watermark cannot be recovered. Screening tools may fail to notice that a protein was ever marked. Critics also warn that a watermark only identifies the source after the fact. It does not stop a malicious actor from making a dangerous protein in the first place. Despite these limits, many scientists see value in the approach, and A watermark may discourage casual misuse. It may also help institutions track unauthorized access to protein-design software. More importantly, the debate has pushed the research community to strengthen oversight. It has also pushed them to share screening standards. And it has pushed them to involve security experts earlier in the design process. As one biosecurity specialist put it, the goal is not a perfect technical fix. The goal is a layered defense, and such a defense makes dangerous misuse harder, riskier, and easier to detect.

sections.title: Watermarking AI-Designed Proteins: A Partial Safeguard
sections.passage:
Artificial intelligence has given scientists an unprecedented ability to design proteins that do not exist in nature, molecules that could yield life-saving drugs or, in the wrong hands, dangerous biological agents. To reduce the risk of misuse, researchers at Google DeepMind have developed a way to embed hidden signatures, or watermarks, into AI-generated proteins without significantly altering their function. The technique, called SynthIDBio, aims to make it easier to trace the origin of a designed protein and to flag suspicious designs for closer scrutiny.

The approach comes in two forms. The first, SynthIDBio-sequence, subtly biases the amino acid choices made by a protein-design program according to a secret key. Anyone who knows the key can later assess how likely a given sequence was produced under that bias. The second, SynthIDBio-structure, introduces minuscule adjustments to the predicted three-dimensional arrangement of atoms, adjustments that a detector can recognize but that are too small to distort the protein's shape. In tests, the systems identified more than 99% of watermarked proteins while correctly ignoring 99.9% of unmarked ones.

Experts describe the work as an impressive technical achievement, yet they caution that it is not ready for widespread use. The watermarks are, in the words of one Microsoft scientist, "effective but brittle." A user can remove a sequence watermark by resequencing the protein, or a structure watermark by adding noise to its spatial coordinates. Once a watermark is stripped away, screening tools have no way to tell that the protein was ever marked.

A further limitation is that watermarking is fundamentally reactive. It can help identify who created a harmful protein after an attack, but it does not stop the protein from being made in the first place. As a specialist in chemical and biological arms control notes, criminals may fear identification, but terrorists seeking a biological weapon are unlikely to care about being traced after a successful strike.

but, the technology may still serve a useful purpose. It could deter casual misuse, help institutions detect unauthorized access to protein-generation software, and discourage misleading claims about how a protein was produced. More broadly, the debate surrounding SynthIDBio has encouraged researchers to strengthen oversight and to involve security experts earlier in the design process.

In the end, no single technical fix can eliminate biosecurity risks. Watermarking is best understood as one layer in a broader defense, making dangerous misuse somewhat harder, riskier, and easier to detect, while human review and international cooperation remain essential.

long_sentences.en: This might deter some criminals, but terrorists looking to create a novel protein for a biological weapon would be less likely to care about being identified after a successful attack, said Max Brackmann , a chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear arms expert at the Spiez Laboratory in Switzerland.

"This has the potential to reduce biosecurity threats, such as unauthorized toxin creation, and may help with database curation, preventing artificial designs from cluttering the standard databases," said Roy Sleator , a biology professor at Munster Technological University in Ireland, who was not involved in the research.

SynthIDBio-sequence subtly influences how the program chooses each amino acid according to a secret watermarking "key." Once the sequence is generated, anyone who knows the hidden code can assess how likely the sequence is to have been created under the key's bias.
